title: US charges Irishman with destroying a $60 million Air Force C-130 with an axe
excerpt: The 48-year-old allegedly used an axe, a drill, corrosive gallium and other tools to sabotage the C-130 while it was parked in Ireland.
content_html:
An Irishman could go to prison for up to 10 years for allegedly destroying a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130H while it was parked for an en route stop at Shannon Airport in Ireland earlier this year. 

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced charges against Daithi O’Corrain, 48, for destroying government property. FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr. said O’Corrain allegedly spent months researching where to infiltrate the airport, how to break into the C-130, which systems to sabotage, and what tools to do it with.

“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” Barnacle said in a Justice Department press release. 

Sabotage

On April 11, at about 4:39 a.m. local time, O’Corrain breached the airport’s security perimeter, according to the indictment. He allegedly broke the locking mechanism on the rear crew door of the C-130, located on the side of the fuselage, then barricaded himself inside and covered all the windows, except the cockpit windows, using the flight crew’s hammocks.

“O’Corrain attached straps, brackets, and screws to various fixed parts of the aircraft’s interior in order to secure the aircraft’s doors; he also placed ball bearings mixed with epoxy into the aircraft’s door tracks in order to prevent the doors from opening and closing,” the indictment read.

The Irishman then allegedly cut wire bundles and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, destroyed every gauge in the cockpit, and punctured air ducts. He also allegedly burned through parts of the C-130H with gallium, “a highly corrosive metal that is a liquid at room temperature, and which eats through aluminum in minutes and causes long-term corrosion to steel,” the indictment said.

After about five hours, the flight crew showed up at about 9:40 a.m., when they spotted O’Corrain through the cockpit window. They flagged Shannon Airport security, only to witness O’Corrain allegedly climb out of a hatch in the airplane’s roof and smash up the exterior with an axe.

O’Corrain was also accused of pouring “unknown substances,” ball bearings, and other objects into the C-130’s fuel tanks to contaminate them before Irish police used portable stairs to climb onto the aircraft’s wing and arrest him.

Months of Preparation

According to the indictment, April 11 was the culmination of months of preparation where O’Corrain researched the C-130’s layout online, ordered gallium, bought tools and equipment, looked for places to sneak onto the airport, and subscribed to an aircraft tracking app that notified him when the C-130 arrived.

That research was evident in the work, the indictment said: O’Corrain allegedly knew how best to destroy the C-130’s critical components; which wires to cut; how to break into the aircraft; and how to crimp rather than cut the liquid oxygen line. If cut, it could have led to “a massive explosion,” the indictment said.

C-130s are tough aircraft that have flown in combat since the late 1950s, but O’Corrain’s alleged sabotage was irreparable, and this tail will never fly again, the indictment said.

Not the first airfield break-in

Photos identify the stricken aircraft as tail number 91-1653, assigned to the Missouri Air National Guard’s 139th Airlift Wing. The wing currently flies the older C-130H model, though Missouri legislators have sought to replace them with newer C-130Js.

Shannon Airport is a major gateway for U.S. aircraft heading to and from the Middle East and Europe, which has angered some Irish who oppose the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran. 

Top Stories This Week

“It’s a contentious issue in Ireland; many people are furious in terms of the U.S.’s use of the airport and they want the Irish government to stop the U.S. from using that airport,” RTÉ News journalist Tommy Meskill told U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich in an August interview. “If the Irish government were to stop the U.S. military from using Shannon, how much of an effect would that have on the U.S. military?”

“It’s a very important logistics hub; it allows America to project power and keep threats at bay from all over the world,” said Grynkewich, the head of U.S. European Command and NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe. “There are some significant security implications to losing access there.” 

O’Corrain is just the latest alleged intruder at Shannon Airport. The indictment cited three other individuals who were arrested on May 1, 2025, after driving a van through the perimeter fence. About two weeks later, another three people spray-painted a U.S. military aircraft, while three more people were detained in November after driving onto a restricted area where a U.S. military C-40 transport was parked.
